instruction: Compare the original and rewrite directly. Independently identify substantive reasoning relations in the original and check all against the rewrite, including omissions, additions, conditions, timing, actors, causal direction, and scope. Return status preserved only when all substantive reasoning survives. Use changed for a material change and uncertain for unresolved meaning. Give concrete evidence for your assessment. Wording and presentation order may differ. Give a short explanation referring to specific parts of the two texts.

documents.original:
Keep a pencil and reusable name cards by the rack so a maker can claim a board before a dozen similar bowls land beside it. If a shelf is too deep to reach across from one side, leave access behind it so nobody has to lean over a row of fresh rims. A small lamp aimed along the back of a dim shelf makes an empty spot easier to distinguish from a space occupied by a low dish. Leave an example board on the teaching table with the pots spaced for a hand to pass between them. Beginners can see how much room to allow before they load their own.

Take warped or splintered boards out of the supply as soon as someone spots them, before another student sets a flat platter on an uneven base. Let members nominate someone to check their work during an absence, giving staff a known person to ask if a piece needs attention.
documents.rewrite:
A maker should be able to put their name on a board before a dozen bowls that look much the same end up next to it. A pencil and a stack of reusable name cards beside the rack make that easy. If a shelf is deeper than someone can reach from the front, keep a way clear to the back. They can then reach their pot without leaning across freshly made rims. On a dark shelf, aim a small light along the back so people can tell whether a gap is really empty or holds a shallow dish.

Set up a board on the teaching table with a hand's breadth between the pots. Before loading their own boards, beginners can see the gap they need to leave for a hand to pass through. As soon as anyone notices a board has warped or started to splinter, pull it from the stack before the next student puts a flat platter on that uneven surface. Members who will be away can name someone to look in on their pots, so staff know whom to ask if a piece needs attention.

documents.original:
Put the number of available chairs against each date on a shared booking calendar so organizers can see whether a request will fit. Ask for the pickup and return times when a booking is made, since a Saturday evening event may mean the chairs are still out on Sunday morning. Have each organizer name someone reachable during the event. A driver running late can call the person with the keys. Give a chair with a loose hinge or missing foot a conspicuous repair tag and a separate storage spot, keeping it out of the next delivery.

Allow time between bookings to check and clean a returned batch before another group expects to collect it. Let a borrower nominate another person to make the return so the chairs can get back on time even when the event organizer has to leave early.
documents.rewrite:
When organizers look up a date on the shared booking calendar, they should be able to see how many chairs are free and judge whether there are enough for their event. Have them give both collection and return times when they book. Chairs picked up for Saturday evening might still be with that group on Sunday morning. Leave a gap between one booking and the next so there's time to inspect and clean the chairs that come back before the next group arrives to collect them.

Ask organizers who will have the keys and be available by phone during the event, so a driver who's behind schedule knows whom to call. Give borrowers the option of designating someone else to bring the chairs back. That way the return can happen on time even if the organizer has to leave early. If a chair has a wobbly hinge or has lost a foot, attach a repair tag that's hard to miss and store it apart from the others so it stays out of the next delivery.

documents.original:
For overlapping conversation, give the two voices separate lines where both are intelligible. Visitors can see that the remarks were made together. Provide a text-size control at each station and let visitors try it on a sample caption before starting a long interview. Start a fresh listening session with captions visible so a visitor can read the opening words without searching through settings. Give long interviews a short list of topics with jump points, letting someone go straight to the passage about the old school or the flood.

Keep optional background notes in the interview listing. Visitors can look up an unfamiliar local custom without losing their place in the speaker's sentence. For an exhibit that plays on a loop, display the interview title alongside the captions so someone arriving midway can place the story.
documents.rewrite:
Have the captions showing whenever a new listening session opens. That lets a visitor catch the first words without hunting for a setting. At every station, offer a sample caption on which visitors can adjust the type size before settling into a long interview. When two people speak at once and you can make out both voices, put each on a line of its own so readers can tell the comments came at the same time.

For longer interviews, a brief topic list with links into the recording lets a listener go directly to the account of the flood or the old school. Put background notes in the interview listing for anyone who wants them. A visitor curious about a local custom can look it up and keep their place in the sentence. When an exhibit repeats on a loop, show the interview's title next to the captions so even a visitor who walks in halfway through knows which story they're hearing.

documents.original:
Model both a friendly invitation and a friendly decline during the welcome. Guests get to hear how either answer can end comfortably. Announce the type of dance before the music starts so a beginner has time to decide whether to get up for it. Show an easy version of a turn that keeps both feet close to the floor, giving anyone who finds spinning uncomfortable a way through the figure. Keep the teacher's face and feet well lit during demonstrations so people can use visual cues when the room is noisy.

Include the door price and payment options in the invitation so people can arrive with the fare in hand and head straight in to meet the host. Invite people to chat briefly over a break with the music turned down. Someone who sat out a few songs can still get to know the group.
documents.rewrite:
Put the admission price and ways to pay on the invitation. Guests can have their money ready at the door and go straight in to meet the host. As you welcome everyone, act out inviting someone to dance and politely turning an invitation down, so newcomers hear how the exchange can end on friendly terms whichever answer they give. Name each dance before its music begins to give beginners a moment to decide if they'd like to get up.

During demonstrations, light the teacher's feet and face well enough for people to follow by sight even when it's noisy. Demonstrate a simpler turn with both feet staying low, so people who find spinning uncomfortable can still do the figure. At a break, lower the music and invite everyone to talk for a few minutes. Guests who've sat out several songs will have a chance to get acquainted too.

documents.original:
Ask bakers to wrap a few small portions from each loaf so someone who lives alone can bring home several kinds without wasting bread. Set out paper bags big enough for a few slices and a pencil for writing on them, so people can tell their selections apart once they're home. Ask each baker how they like to eat their bread the following day. A reheating or toasting suggestion makes a less familiar loaf easier to choose. A child who wants to help could draw a little portrait of a loaf for the table, giving families something to do together without handling the samples.

Invite contributors to choose a home for their spare bread in advance, allowing the closing crew to pass it along with the baker's agreement. Keep a sheet where visitors can request a bread they remember fondly, giving a neighbor who knows how to bake it an idea for the next gathering.
documents.rewrite:
Have each baker wrap a few small servings of every loaf they bring. A person who lives on their own can then take a variety home without ending up with bread that goes to waste. Supply paper bags that will hold a few slices apiece and a pencil to label them, so visitors can still tell which bread is which when they get home. As people choose, ask bakers how they enjoy their bread a day later. Knowing that the baker likes a particular loaf toasted or warmed up can make an unfamiliar kind easier to pick.

If a child is keen to help, invite them to sketch a loaf to display on the table. The family can do that together and leave the samples untouched. Ask contributors to decide in advance where they'd like any extra bread to go, so the people closing up have the baker's agreement when they pass it on. Give visitors a sheet to write down breads they remember with affection. A neighbor who knows how to make one may take the suggestion up for the next swap.

documents.original:
Let a gardener contribute an unfinished pencil study near the front. A few searching lines make putting an imperfect mark in a public book feel easier. A small cardboard viewfinder helps someone faced with a whole border pick a patch of stems that fits on the page. Choose a binding that lies open by itself so a visitor can hold a pencil in one hand and steady a child's hand with the other. Leave space for the plant's garden location beside a drawing, helping another visitor track down an intriguing seed head for a closer look.

Ask visitors to turn the book toward the plant when taking a reference photo, keeping other guests out of the frame in a busy glasshouse. Keep a few pieces of scrap paper in the pencil tray for people who want to try a mark privately before committing it to the shared book.
documents.rewrite:
Invite a gardener to leave a partly finished pencil sketch on one of the first pages. Seeing a few tentative strokes there may help someone feel comfortable making an imperfect mark in a book everyone can see. Tuck a few scraps of paper into the pencil tray too, so a visitor can try out a stroke in private before drawing it in the book. For someone wondering how to fit a whole border onto a page, offer a little cardboard viewfinder to frame a manageable cluster of stems.

Use a binding that stays open on its own. A visitor can then draw with one hand while steadying a child's hand with the other. Beside each sketch, leave room to say where in the garden the plant grows. Someone intrigued by a drawing of a seed head can find it and look more closely. Ask anyone taking a reference photo to face the book toward the plant. That keeps other guests out of the frame in a busy glasshouse.

documents.original:
Give each alteration note a garment name and the wearer's left or right side. The person sewing tomorrow should be able to pick it up without a demonstration. Reserve a rail for garments ready to go onstage, keeping them out of the alterations pile when the room is cleared at the end. Keep an easy-to-read clock within the fitter's sight so they can pace an appointment without repeatedly looking away from the performer. Mark borrowed pieces on the rail with the owner's alteration limits, saving a volunteer from shortening a hem that must be returned intact.

Circle any change that needs another fitting and agree on a return time with the wearer, while their schedule and the garment are both to hand. Write down the agreed priorities if there's more sewing than the team can finish, so a costume needed at tomorrow's rehearsal gets attention in time.
documents.rewrite:
Position a legible clock where the fitter can keep track of the appointment without having to turn away from the performer again and again. On every alteration note, identify the garment and specify left or right from the wearer's point of view. Tomorrow's volunteer should be able to do the sewing without anyone having to show them what was meant. While borrowed garments are on the rail, label them with the limits their owners have set. No one should discover after shortening a hem that the owner needs it back at its original length.

If a change calls for another fitting, circle it and settle on a time for the wearer to come back while you still have the garment and the wearer's schedule in front of you. When the sewing exceeds what the team can get through, record which jobs you've agreed to tackle first so a costume needed for rehearsal tomorrow is dealt with in time. Give stage-ready pieces a rail of their own so they stay clear of the pile awaiting alterations during the end-of-evening cleanup.

documents.original:
Place a demonstration board in a corner away from active games, giving a helper room to show a position without gathering a crowd around someone else's match. Offer a small sign that a seated player can turn toward the door when they'd welcome an opponent, taking the guesswork out of joining a stranger. Keep a written waiting list during busy periods, letting visitors sit down to read instead of hovering over games that look nearly finished. Set up a place for post-game discussion a little away from the quiet boards, since a lively analysis can last much longer than the game itself.

Encourage a quiet word with the host if a disagreement develops, giving players a way to settle a rules question without drawing in the whole room. Leave a pencil and paper for recording an unfinished position, allowing two visitors to pause a game without having to keep the board occupied.
documents.rewrite:
Give someone sitting at a board a small sign to face toward the entrance when they'd like an opponent. A newcomer can then tell whether a stranger is open to a game. When the room gets busy, put names on a written waiting list so visitors can sit and read while they wait, without hovering over a match that seems about to end. Keep a demonstration board in a corner clear of games in progress. A helper can show someone a position there without bringing onlookers around another pair's match.

Give players a spot a little way from the quiet boards to talk over a finished game. An animated discussion of the moves can run much longer than the match. If players disagree, encourage them to speak quietly to the host so they can resolve a question about the rules without involving everyone else. Keep a pencil and paper handy for two visitors to note the position if they need to pause their game. That frees the board for someone else in the meantime.
